title: City-funded charities that closed: what the State was told and where the assets went
question: When a City-funded charity in this batch wound up, did its papers to the Attorney General and its final federal return say the same thing about its remaining assets?
finding: 3 organizations in the batch filed dissolution papers with the registry or a final federal return. Oakes Childrens Center: no dissolution document on its registry list; final return for the period ended 2022-07-31: to Community Behavioral Health Services (1380 Howard St): Cash and Accounts receivables $19,309; Buildings, net accumulated depreciation $12,792; Investments $2,924; Accounts payable $195,474; Notes payable and other liabilities $647,220; Net assets $-807,623. Urban Ed Academy: 2026-03-18 dissolution request; 2026-10-14 registry asked for more before it will waive; no final return on disk. California Partnership For Safe Communit: 2025-08-06 dissolution request; 2026-02-12 waiver: no assets; 2026-04-30 dissolution documents; 2026-10-16 file closed; final return for the period ended 2025-06-30: to University of Pennsylvania (3451 Walnut Street): Balance in Bank Accounts $206,664.
how: The registry's own document list gives each dissolution request, waiver and closure letter. A final return is one the IRS e-file data marks as final; its Schedule N (liquidation) rows are read from the return's XML. City payments are the payee's last two fiscal years with payments.
limits: Schedule N is filled in by the organization's preparer; a recipient named there may be the agency that took over its clients rather than a body that received money. The registry lists only documents it has published; a letter it received but did not post would not show. A "no assets" waiver is the registry's acceptance of the balance sheet it was sent, not an audit of it.
